The bed helped people stay asleep. It did not help them get there, and it gave them nothing they could use the next day.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Sixteen people, all young adults, one rocking night each. Nobody knows whether the gain lasts a week, or fades as the body gets used to the movement. Insomnia comes in many shapes and causes, and people sensitive to sensation might find a moving bed distracting rather than calming. Nothing here says how older people, or people who are more seriously ill, would respond.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The bed could not talk the worry down. It just kept time, and the sleeping brain followed.

recall.q: The rocking bed helped one half of these people's sleep problem and not the other. Which half — and what did the brain recordings suggest was going on?
recall.a: It helped them stay asleep: 34 percent less time awake mid-night, less broken sleep, and a 25 percent better rating in the morning. It did not help them fall asleep faster, and it did not improve memory. The recordings showed spindles clustering at the bed's turning points, so the motion seems to pace the rhythms that hold sleep rather than start it.

cards.title: A longer exhale made people take the riskier bet
cards.body: Breathe in for two counts and out for eight, and people in a brain scanner chose the riskier option more often. Losses did not scare them less — their reaction to possible losses barely changed. The long exhale made their brains respond more to the reward.
cards.evidence: single study · n=41 healthy adults · fMRI with breathing, heart, skin and pupil monitoring

sections.text:
Breathe in for two counts. Breathe out for eight. That was the whole experiment in a study just published in Neuron, and it was enough to change what people were willing to bet on.

Forty-one healthy people followed breathing cues on a screen while making risky choices — options where the better prize was less sure. Sometimes they breathed at their own normal pace. Sometimes they stretched the out-breath to four times the length of the in-breath. When the out-breath was long, their heart rate slowed, and they picked the riskier option more often.

The interesting part is why. You would guess that a calm body makes losses feel less scary. It didn't. People reacted to possible losses about the same under both breathing patterns. What changed was the other side: their brains reacted more strongly to possible rewards. Slow breathing did not shrink the downside. It brightened the upside.

Two brain areas worked harder during the long out-breaths — the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. Both help process rewards. Both also help control heart rate variability, the tiny differences in timing between one heartbeat and the next, which the long exhale increased. That overlap is the study's quiet point: the parts of the brain that judge how good a prize looks are tied to how your heart is beating.

For a long time, decision-making was treated as something that happens in the head, with the body along for the ride. This work belongs to a growing counter-view — neurovisceral models, meaning models where your body state actively shapes your thinking instead of just reporting to it. Signals travel up as well as down.

What is new here is the direction of control. Breathing is one of the few body rhythms you can take over on purpose. If a longer exhale nudges the brain's reward system, you have a handle — simple, free, learnable — on a process that usually runs without you. The researchers see clinical promise in that, especially for anxiety and depression, conditions that involve both poor body regulation and changed responses to reward. They also want to test it on food, since eating is driven hard by reward and body state.

But notice what the study actually says before you reach for it. It does not show that slow breathing makes decisions better. It shows that slow breathing makes rewards pull harder — useful when fear is holding you back, unhelpful when the prize is a bad idea. The calm you build before a big choice is not a neutral clearing of the mind. It presses one side of the scale.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: Forty-one healthy adults followed cues on a screen, switching between their own natural pace and a 2:8 pattern — in for two counts, out for eight. Brain activity was tracked with functional MRI, a scan that follows blood flow to show which areas are working. The team also recorded breathing, heart activity, skin conductance — a measure of sweat — and pupil size. That wide net was the point: measuring several body signals at once let them check whether the long exhale did anything beyond slowing the heart.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One study, 41 people, all healthy. The link between slow breathing and bolder choices is an association seen in a lab, and the researchers say the next step is checking whether it holds in clinical groups. Park, one of the researchers, calls the result "scientific proof" that breath is a reliable way to control our decisions. That is a big claim to rest on 41 people. Hold it loosely until someone repeats the study.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Calm did not make the danger smaller. It made the prize louder.

recall.q: Slow breathing made people choose the riskier option more often. What changed in the brain to produce that, and what did not change?
recall.a: Their reaction to possible losses stayed about the same — the long exhale did not dull their fear of the downside. What grew was the brain's response to possible rewards. The upside got louder, not the downside quieter.

cards.title: Three in four US books were sold door to door
cards.body: America barely had bookstores: 1,090 in 1859, and still only 3,501 by 1914. So until the end of the century, three quarters of books in the country were sold by men knocking on doors, taking orders for books nobody had printed yet. Mark Twain made his name inside that system, then lost his money betting on the machine.

sections.text:
A man knocks on your door. He is selling a book that does not exist yet. You give him your name, he writes down the order, and the book is printed only later — once enough names have been collected.

In nineteenth-century America, that was not a strange way to buy a book. It was the normal way. Until the end of the century, three out of every four books sold in the United States were sold exactly like that: door to door, in advance, by men called canvassers.

Jeff Jarvis, writing at Literary Hub, tells the story of how mass media was born. The door-to-door salesman sits near the middle of it. The technical half of the story is the typesetting machine — the machine that arranges the letters before a page can be printed. Once publishers had machines that could turn out books in bulk, they hit a new problem, and it was not a printing problem. They could make far more books than they had any way to sell.

Look at where those books were supposed to go. In 1859, all of America had 1,090 bookstores. By 1914, more than half a century later, there were still only 3,501. If readers could not find books, books had to find their readers. So: the knock on the door. The best-seller, that modern thing, was not born inside a shop. It was built by men walking.

Mark Twain is what Jarvis calls the Zelig of this story — the figure who turns up in every scene. He set type at his brother's ratty newspaper. He was a tramp printer, moving from shop to shop for work, watching printing technology explode around him. He became one of the first best-selling authors, and a real celebrity. He became a publisher, trying to work out what a business model for books might even look like. And he put his money into the Paige Compositor, a typesetting machine that lost to the Linotype. It bankrupted him.

That last scene is the sharp one. Twain bet on the machine and was ruined. What carried his books to readers was not a machine. It was the canvasser: the order taken in advance, the slow human work of collecting names one door at a time. He got the technology wrong and the selling right. Only one of those made his name.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: 1859: 1,090 bookstores in all of America. 1914: still only 3,501.
Canvassers took the order before the book existed — printing waited until enough names came in.
Twain stands at every point of the chain — typesetter, tramp printer, best-seller, publisher, and the investor the Paige Compositor bankrupted.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The machine could make a million books. Only a person walking could find a million readers.

recall.q: Printing machines could suddenly produce books in volume. Why didn't that create the best-seller by itself — and what did?
recall.a: Because there was almost nowhere to sell them: 1,090 bookstores in 1859, and still only 3,501 by 1914. Printing was solved long before selling was, so books went out to find readers instead — door-to-door canvassers taking orders before printing, which is how three quarters of American books sold until the end of the century.

cards.title: The poet Dorothea Lasky: every line could be a question
cards.body: Paris was in its warmest June on record — burnt lawns, wilted flowers, no one able to think clearly. Inside, over pink fruit water and dark brown cola, the poet Dorothea Lasky talked about her new collection, Mother. There is no punctuation anywhere in the book. Even a question gets no question mark.

sections.text:
Lasky has written ten books of poems and essays, on everything from The Shining to fashion to roses to anger. Color runs through all of it. "Color makes a mood that can wash over anything," she once wrote. Mother is made of blues, grays, browns and blacks. When a bright color does arrive it feels wrong: red turns monstrous, orange warns that a death is close. The moods that wash over this book are anger, closed-in panic, and fear for a child.

It began as letters. Pregnant with her third child, Lasky set out to remake a book by Bernadette Mayer. Mayer wrote it during her own third pregnancy. Prose letters — this time to Lasky's father. They turned into poems at once, the way everything she writes does. Then her mother died while the book was still being edited, and the poems changed who they were speaking to.

Mother and father carry the weight of God and the Devil in a poem, she says. You cannot ignore them. In her work the mother is a moral measuring stick and also its opposite. The spotless, wholly good mother is an invention of patriarchy — a world arranged on men's terms. Her real subject is making that figure messy. The poems are not a diary. A reader once told her he knew all about her mother, the one who put fruit in jars to last the winter. Her mother never did that. The line came from a man with dementia.

The darkest poems face the medical system. Her point is not that doctors are cruel. It is that a patient cannot leave until the hospital lets her go, and a good patient does not ask questions. In pregnancy the system holds the thing you love most. You agree to anything as long as the baby is fine. Systems feed on the love people will do anything for.

Under all of it sits one stubborn idea: a poem is a body. In high school Lasky worked in a lab, calming flies with carbon dioxide and lifting out their brains under a microscope. Horrible, she says — and something of it is in this book. Painters get credit for canvas and paint. Language is material too, and a poem is full of meat.

The last line of the first poem changed twice. In the magazine it was a promise: you will save it, just like the others. In the book Lasky put back her first draft — "But will you save it". Alone in a magazine, that sureness worked, she says; at the opening of a book it gives too much away. And saving is never settled. You can save someone once. You cannot save them forever, because they are going to die.

There is no question mark. She made that rule as a student — no mark at the end of any line — while teaching poems to second graders who were corrected all day for missing commas. A full stop at the end of a line is dramatic, she says, and the line break has already ended things. So the question stays quiet. She likes the thought that every line could be one.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A promise turned into a question is not weaker. It is more honest.

recall.q: In the magazine, the first poem ended on a promise — you will save it, just like the others. In the book, Lasky put the question back. Why?
recall.a: Because saving is never settled: you can save someone once, but not forever, since they will die. She also felt the flat promise, which worked when the poem stood alone, gave too much away at the opening of a book.

cards.title: Why breaking up Google could strengthen Apple
cards.body: Google was found guilty of breaking antitrust law — the rules against one company owning a market — with its advertising business. Again, it will not be broken up. Campaigners on the left and right are angry. Semafor's answer: antitrust is a balloon. Squeeze one giant and the power bulges out somewhere else.

sections.text:
The warning: the 2012 e-book case. The US Justice Department sued Apple and big publishers for fixing e-book prices. They had done it to fight Amazon, which sold e-books at a loss. Publishers settled; Apple fought and lost. Amazon was left to rule book publishing, prices rose anyway, and bookstores closed.

Spin Android off from Google, the same logic says, and cheap phones cost more while Apple — already too powerful — grows stronger. In the Google search case, Judge Amit Mehta wrote that courts must craft remedies with "a healthy dose of humility."

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A court sees one company, one case. It cannot redraw a whole industry, so a breakup often moves the monopoly instead of ending it. Semafor's fix: fund university research, where new tech startups come from, plus tax breaks and grants for founders and higher taxes on big multinationals.

recall.q: Apple lost the 2012 e-book case in court. Why does Semafor call that a warning, not a win?
recall.a: Stopping Apple's price-fixing left Amazon with no real rival in books. Bookstores closed and prices for readers rose anyway. Curbing one giant handed the market to another.

cards.title: Patience follows social freedom, not willpower
cards.body: We call waiting for a better tomorrow willpower — a trait some people simply have more of. But across 202,070 people in 22 countries, what lined up best at the country level was something else: how freely people there can make new friends and leave old ones. Japan and Hong Kong, the supposed champions of long-term thinking, were among the least likely to believe that sacrificing now pays off later.
cards.evidence: two studies · n=202,070 across 22 countries + n=785 Japan/US · self-report · correlational

sections.text:
The group is going out tonight. You stay home with the textbook.

We have a fast name for that: willpower. Self-control. Something inside you, a muscle some people are born with more of. Stretch the idea to whole countries and you get a familiar claim — East Asian cultures think long-term because of Confucian values. The claim is so old that when researchers first named this trait, they called it "Confucian dynamism."

Then someone put the trait on a world map, and the ranking came out backwards.

Kuan-Ju Huang, at Kyoto University, took the question to 202,070 people in 22 countries. He compared those countries on relational mobility — how freely people there can make new friends and leave old ones. It runs high in North and Latin America. It runs low across much of East Asia, where social ties are more fixed: hard to enter a new group, hard to leave a bad one.

The freer the social world, the more willing people were to trade happiness now for happiness later. Japan and Hong Kong sat near the bottom — least likely to believe the sacrifice would ever be repaid. National wealth, income gaps and how much a culture prizes the individual did not consistently predict this, once he corrected for how differently people answer surveys from country to country.

The mechanism is not a moral one. Waiting is a bet. You hand over something certain today for something you cannot see yet. That only makes sense if you trust the future to arrive — if you believe your life can still move somewhere better. A flexible social world hands you exactly that belief. When you can leave a group that is going nowhere and join one that isn't, your life feels steerable.

So Huang looked for the feelings sitting in between. His models found two. The chain ran: more social freedom, then a stronger sense of control and more optimism, then more willingness to wait. A second study of 785 people, split between Japan and the United States, produced the same chain with fuller questions. And the people who said they could delay happiness reported better well-being on every measure, most of all a sense of meaning and purpose.

The old story survives because from the outside the two look the same. People in fixed social worlds do endure. They study, they save, they put things off. Huang's point is that they endure without the belief attached — the sacrifice happens, the expectation of being repaid does not. We watch the waiting and credit the character. The waiting was never the rare part.

sections.label: The studies
sections.text: Study one used the Global Flourishing Study: 202,070 people in 22 countries, each rating a single sentence — "I am always able to give up some happiness now for greater happiness later" — alongside measures of happiness and life satisfaction, meaning and purpose, balance and harmony, and optimism. Country scores for relational mobility, wealth, inequality and individualism were laid over the top. Study two was an online survey of 785 people, split roughly evenly between Japan and the United States. It swapped the single questions for full multi-question scales of delaying happiness, optimism, sense of control, and how flexible a person's own social circle is.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a snapshot, not a film. Everything was measured at one moment, so it cannot show that social freedom creates the optimism rather than the other way round. Relational mobility scores existed for only 15 of the 22 countries. In the second study people rated the flexibility of their own circle, which may say more about their personal situation than about the society around them. And in the first study, the whole measure of delaying happiness was one sentence.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Someone who will not wait may not be weak. Their future may just be a worse bet.

recall.q: Japan and Hong Kong are famous for long-term thinking, yet they scored among the least willing to delay happiness. What explains that, on this account?
recall.a: Waiting is a bet on the future, and it only pays if the future feels reachable. Where social ties are fixed — hard to leave a group, hard to join a new one — people feel less control over where their life goes and less optimism about it, so the sacrifice does not look like it will be repaid. They still endure; they just don't expect the payoff.
